fetched_contents.text: Low velocity impact resistance and energy absorption of environmentally friendly expanded cork core-carbon fiber sandwich composites Abstract This study investigates the use of expanded cork (a 100% natural lightweight agglomerate material) as a core material in composite sandwich structures with carbon fiber face sheets. The characterization performed focused particularly on energy absorption capability. Rohacell® 110 IG, a synthetic foam commonly used as a core material in high performance aerospace applications, was also used and characterized to compare the energy absorbing characteristics of the sandwich composites. Bending tests were done to examine the stiffness of the sandwich beams. Wavenumber and damping tests were performed to characterize the acoustic and vibrational damping properties of the composites. Both full penetration and partial penetration low velocity impact tests were completed to determine the damage resistance of the composites. It was seen that when compared to the synthetic foam, expanded cork showed a decrease in bending stiffness, but a large improvement in acoustic, damping, and impact damage resistance characteristics. It seems that expanded cork could be an attractive lightweight sandwich core material that will allow for increased energy absorption and will also reduce the carbon footprint of the structures. Introduction Expanded cork, also referred to as insulation cork or black agglomerate, is a 100% natural material. Expanded cork is a lightweight agglomerate structure that is water resistant and has very low thermal conductivity [1]. Cork is also known for its great recovery capabilities, a property particularly useful in energy absorption that synthetic materials have tried to emulate [1], [2], [3], [4]. Cork is a cellular material that comes from the bark of the Cork Oak found primarily in the Mediterranean region of Europe. The bark is peeled from the tree, and then it grows back over the next 9 years [1]. In this way the tree is not cut down and the resource is completely renewable. To produce traditional cork agglomerates, cork bark is ground up into small granules, exposed to compression, and an artificial binding material which holds the granules together. Unlike standard cork agglomerates, expanded cork exposes the granules to compression along with superheated steam. This steam heats up the particles, expands them up to 30% in volume, and activates the natural resins which naturally bind the granules together [1], [5]. This manufacturing process, which has been around since the late 1800’s [6], causes the cell walls lose thickness and stretch during the expansion. Expanded cork is 100% natural, renewable, and relatively easy to produce, giving it an incredibly small carbon footprint and making it an attractive “green” material. Sandwich structures are composite materials made by adhesively bonding two thin stiff face sheets to a much weaker, thick, lightweight core material. The face sheets resist bending stress while the core material mainly resists shear stress. These structures are similar in principle to I-beams. They use the core material to provide separation of the face sheets to achieve high bending strength while maintaining low weight [7]. Sandwich structures are regularly employed in aerospace in places including wings, cabin doors, cabin walls, flooring, fairings, etc. They can also be found in other industries such as transportation (boats, automobiles, trains) sporting goods (surfboards, skis), wind (turbine and propeller blades), and structural building applications (walls, roofs, supports). One undesirable property of sandwich composites is that they perform poorly with respect to energy absorption. This poor energy absorption can have a number of detrimental effects including radiation of unwanted noise, proliferation of vibrations that can shorten the lifespan of the composite, and a high susceptibility to damage due to impact. In order to improve energy absorption properties of sandwich structures, the effect of different core materials and geometries have been investigated [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13]. The previous studies have shown that increased acoustic and damping capabilities can be obtained by decreasing the shear modulus of the core [9], [13]. High performance sandwich structures commonly used in many applications, specifically in aerospace and transport, often feature carbon fiber face sheets along with a core material that is either honeycomb or high performance synthetic foam. The carbon fiber face sheets are commonly used because of their outstanding specific strength. Rohacell® is known to be one of the most common of the synthetic foams used in aerospace applications. This core material however, is not ideal for energy absorption, performing particularly poorly in acoustic and vibration testing [11], [12], [13]. In today’s world “green” materials are becoming increasingly popular in an attempt to save energy and reduce carbon emissions. There have been a number of studies examining cork agglomerate with artificial binding agents for use in sandwich structures. These works have shown that cork agglomerate has beneficial energy absorption properties including: noise mitigation, damping, and partial penetration low velocity impact [4], [11], [12], [13]. Expanded cork however has significant chemical and structural differences when compared to cork agglomerate which will affect its applicability in various structures. Expanded cork has been implemented mainly as an insulating building material, and thus its thermal properties have been well documented. However, expanded cork has not been properly studied in areas dealing with energy absorption in sandwich constructions. Its full potential for uses in these applications has not been thoroughly investigated. fetched_contents.text: (PDF) A review of low-velocity impact on sandwich structures This contribution is a review of past and current research progress on dynamic response of composites sandwich structures subjected to low-velocity impact. To obtain a comprehensive overview of the current state-of-the-art published works, impact responses on sandwich structures are broadly classified into two main groups, high-velocity and low-velocity impacts, with the focus on low-velocity impact. A summary of some of the commonly used theoretical solutions for low-velocity impact is provided and described in some details. The response of low-velocity impact has been determined based on mass ratio, which is defined as the ratio of the impact mass to effective mass of the structural component. As a result, the response under low-velocity impact was further subdivided into three possible categories, namely, large, small, and medium mass impacts. For each category of impact, currently available suitable solutions are discussed in details. To classify the response of low-velocity impact and also to explore the energy-absorption characteristics as well, the impact duration is identified as the key parameter. The review concludes with detailed discussions on the damage mechanisms and failure criteria for sandwich structures subjected to impact loads. Keywords: Impact damage, Composite sandwich panel, Dynamic response. 1 Introduction Composite sandwich panels are generally made up of two thin but stiff facesheets or skins separated by a lightweight and thick but low modulus core. Thus they are relatively light weight and efficient in supporting transverse loads. Generally, the facesheets are made of light alloys such as aluminium or fibre-reinforced composites while the core materials used in structural applications include honeycomb cores made of Nomex, fiberglass reinforced thermoplastic, aluminium, and foam type cores. The core thicknesses range between 3 and 26 2 mm [1-5]. This combination of materials resulted in a rather competitive structure in application area where specific strength and stiffness are the main focus.Sandwich structures are commonly found in many engineering applications such as the aerospace and aircraft industries, marine industries and wind turbine industries. It is well known thatmost of the in- plane membrane and bending forces are supported by the facesheets while the shear loads are transferred by the core. Although lightweight, composites and composite sandwich structures are susceptible to impact damage, which may severely decrease the structural stiffness, stability and load carrying capacity. Birds or debris from the runaway during aircraft takeoffs and landing are some of common impactors. However, the damage suffered internally by the panel during impact is very difficult to inspect [1-8]. The study of the effects of the impact load on plate structures has a long history of more than 200 years while the first 150 years were devoted almost exclusively to empirical studies of the penetration. Simple semi-empirical or quasi-rational representations of this type of impact began to appear towards the end of the 19th century. The first research work concerning in- plane compressive loads in sandwich structures was the work by Marguerre in 1944 [8]. From that point onwards, research on composites and composite sandwich structures boomed and many books on sandwich structures were published. fetched_contents.text: Low-Velocity Impact Behavior of Foam Core Sandwich Panels with Inter-Ply and Intra-Ply Carbon/Kevlar/Epoxy Hybrid Face Sheets Abstract Sandwich composites are extensively employed in a variety of applications because their bending stiffness affords a greater advantage than composite materials. However, the aspect limiting the application of the sandwich material is its poor impact resistance. Therefore, understanding the impact properties of the sandwich structure will determine the ways in which it can be used under the conditions of impact loading. Sandwich panels with different combinations of carbon/Kevlar woven monolithic face sheets, inter-ply face sheets and intra-ply face sheets were fabricated, using the vacuum-assisted resin transfer process. Instrumented low-velocity impact tests were performed using different energy levels of 5 J, 10 J, 20 J, 30 J and 40 J on a variety of samples and the results were assessed. The damage caused by the modes of failure in the sandwich structure include fiber breakage, matrix cracking, foam cracking and debonding. In sandwich panels with thin face sheets, the maximum peak load was achieved for the inter-ply hybrid foam core sandwich panel in which Kevlar was present towards the outer surface and carbon in the inner surface of the face sheet. At an impact energy of 40 J, the maximum peak load for the inter-ply hybrid foam core sandwich panel was 31.57% higher than for the sandwich structure in which carbon is towards the outer surface and Kevlar is in the inner surface of the face sheet. The intra-ply hybrid foam core sandwich panel subjected to 40 J impact energy demonstrated a 13.17% higher maximum peak load compared to the carbon monolithic face sheet sandwich panel. The experimental measurements and numerical predictions are in close agreement. Keywords: low-velocity impact, hybrid epoxy composite, damage tolerance, carbon, kevlar, inter-ply, intra-ply 1. Introduction Foam core sandwich composites are used in industries such as aerospace, automobile, wind turbines, marine functional materials and even in home appliances because of their high strength to weight ratio, good buckling resistance and tailorable design which remains dimensionally stable across a wide temperature range [1,2,3,4,5]. Sandwich foam core structures have distinct advantages which make them the preferred choice for numerous applications involving bending, buckling and energy absorption applications such as dynamic loading, high- and low-velocity impacts, blasts, crashes, etc. [6]. While sandwich composites are designed to resist bending and buckling loads, they also demonstrate excellent energy absorption capabilities [7,8]. Sandwich structures are extensively used in aerospace applications including Unmanned Arial Vehicles (UAV), wind turbine blades and marine structures which are employed extensively under adverse conditions, including impact loads [9]. Impact failure is a common problem that affects the strength and structural integrity of sandwich composites [10,11]. This issue is usually caused by the degradation of energy absorption competence and structural stiffness. The sandwich structure suffers major damage from the impact load, and the damage progressively increases with repeated loading [12,13]. Therefore, hybrid composites are designed and developed to improve different properties such as impact resistance, thermal conductivity, dielectric breakdown strength, flexural and environmental degradation resistance [14,15,16]. A sandwich composite is a type of lightweight structure that has high specific strength and stiffness. It is also suitable for high in-plane and flexural stiffness. Impact applications are limited in sandwich composites due to the absence of good resistance to localized loading. Different types of core materials are developed and used in the construction of sandwich composites. The core should be a low-cost, lightweight material, with the ability to transmit the shear forces generated by face sheets to the other components of the sandwich [17]. High strength metallic face sheets with a honeycomb core are not ideal for the weight-saving of the sandwich panels [18]. The strong and stiff bonding between the core material and face sheets is necessary to enable the sandwich to bear high loads [19]. Kevlar fibers can improve the impact damage tolerance of the composite materials when used together with carbon fibers [20,21,22,23,24,25]. The sandwich construction is composed of two face sheets, separated by a low-density foam core. In hybrid fiber sandwich structures, two or more types of fibers are used in the face sheets to improve the monolithic face sheet properties [25,26,27,28]. The impact and the failure mechanism for the sandwich structure is a very complex mechanism and continues to remain an active topic under discussion by many researchers [29,30,31,32,33,34,35]. Enhancement of the impact properties of the foam sandwich panels through stitching, Z-pinning, tufting and also by implementing changes in the density of the foam core has been investigated by researchers [36,37,38,39,40]. Fiber-reinforced polymer composites are an excellent substitute for face sheets, more than traditional metallic face sheets owing to their ratios of good stiffness to weight, and strength to weight. Even with low-velocity impact, the minor impact can still induce significant damage to structures [41]. Such types of damage can severely weaken the strength and stiffness of a structure. Thus, it is critical to consider the effect of low-velocity impacts on the carbon/Kevlar-epoxy hybrid face sheets with a foam core. With reference to this, Gustin et al. studied the effect of low-velocity impact using different incident face sheet combinations of the Kevlar/carbon foam core sandwich panels [42]. Cork agglomerate sandwich composites show a mixed but generally favorable low-velocity impact profile in the evidence provided. The direct cork study reports that expanded cork core-carbon fiber sandwiches were tested for energy absorption capability, and compared to Rohacell® 110 IG, a synthetic foam used in high-performance aerospace applications. The study found that expanded cork showed a decrease in bending stiffness compared to synthetic foam, but a large improvement in acoustic, damping, and impact damage resistance characteristics [N1-F1]. That same source also notes that cork is a 100% natural lightweight agglomerate material and that its recovery properties are useful in energy absorption, while synthetic materials have tried to emulate them [N1-F1]. In the context of low-velocity impact, the evidence says that at this impact energy the sandwich plates absorb more energy because the cork core deforms due to its low stiffness and contributes to energy absorption [N1-R2].

On force-displacement response, the direct evidence is somewhat indirect. The cork study emphasizes energy absorption capability and damage resistance, and it describes bending tests for stiffness and wavenumber/damping tests for acoustic/vibrational damping [N1-F1]. It does not provide a full force-displacement curve in the excerpt, but it does indicate that cork’s low stiffness allows it to deform and absorb energy during impact [N1-R2]. That implies a relatively soft or gradual force-displacement response compared to stiffer cores, which is consistent with energy absorption through core deformation.

Stiffness and damping behavior are explicitly separated in the evidence. Bending tests were used to examine stiffness, and wavenumber and damping tests were performed to characterize acoustic and vibrational damping [N1-F1]. The result was a decrease in bending stiffness for cork compared to synthetic foam, but large improvements in damping and acoustic characteristics [N1-F1]. This means cork is less stiff during impact but better at dissipating vibrational energy, which can reduce noise and residual vibrations after impact [N1-F1]. The failure mode relevance is that lower stiffness can help spread the load over more core material, while damping helps mitigate the amplitude of vibrations and residual damage.

Failure modes observed in tests include core deformation, damage resistance, and partial penetration low-velocity impact behavior. The cork study states that cork agglomerates have beneficial energy absorption properties including noise mitigation, damping, and partial penetration low-velocity impact [N1-F1]. A separate low-velocity impact review notes that common failure modes in sandwich panels include matrix cracking, delaminations, foam crushing, or face–core debonding and perforation [N3-R3]. For cork, the direct evidence points to deformation and damage resistance rather than brittle fracture; the cork study emphasizes that expanded cork showed improved impact damage resistance characteristics [N1-F1]. The relevance to performance is that cork’s failure mechanism is more progressive and damage-tolerant than brittle failure modes, which can help preserve structural integrity after impact [N1-F1].

Overall, the evidence supports a performance profile for cork agglomerate sandwich composites under low-velocity impact that is energy-absorptive, damping-enhancing, and damage-resistant, but with lower stiffness than synthetic foams [N1-F1][N1-R2]. The force-displacement response is implied to be less rigid and more energy-absorptive, while stiffness and damping behavior are directionally opposite: lower stiffness, better damping [N1-F1]. Failure modes are consistent with deformation and damage tolerance rather than catastrophic brittle failure [N1-F1][N3-R3].

Other materials compared in low-velocity impact performance in the evidence include foam cores, honeycomb cores, rigid foams, and fiber-reinforced composites, with some direct benchmarking against synthetic foams and fiber-reinforced face sheets. The foam-core evidence is especially explicit: one study reports that the intra-ply hybrid foam core sandwich panel subjected to 40 J impact energy demonstrated a 13.17% higher maximum peak load compared to the carbon monolithic face sheet sandwich panel [N4-F3]. Another study notes that foam-core sandwich panels are extensively used because of their high strength-to-weight ratio, good buckling resistance, and tailorable design, but that they still suffer major damage from impact loads that progressively increase with repeated loading [N4-F3]. The review on low-velocity impact states that the peak load and stiffness of the sandwich structure increase with relative density, panel thickness, and impact energy [N2-R3]. This implies that stiffer cores can achieve higher stiffness but may not necessarily absorb more energy; in other words, stiffness is one dimension of performance while energy absorption is another [N2-R3]. The review also notes that sandwich structures are generally made of thin stiff face sheets and a lightweight, thick low-modulus core [N2-F2], reinforcing that core stiffness is a core-dependent property.

Energy absorption values are more directly visible for foam cores. The foam-core study reports impact energy levels of 5 J, 10 J, 20 J, 30 J, and 40 J, and it links impact energy to peak load and damage modes such as fiber breakage, matrix cracking, foam cracking, and debonding [N4-F3]. The evidence also states that sandwich structures are extensively used in aerospace, automobile, wind turbines, marine functional materials, and home appliances because of their bending stiffness advantages [N4-F3]. In comparison, the cork study says that expanded cork showed a large improvement in acoustic, damping, and impact damage resistance characteristics compared to synthetic foam [N1-F1], but it does not provide a direct energy-absorption number for cork. Instead, it emphasizes energy absorption capability and noise mitigation [N1-F1].

Failure behavior differs across materials. The foam-core study reports damage modes including fiber breakage, matrix cracking, foam cracking, and debonding [N4-F3]. The low-velocity impact review notes that common failure mechanisms include matrix cracking, delaminations, foam crushing, or face–core debonding and perforation [N3-R3]. These are consistent with brittle or progressive damage in foam and hybrid face sheet systems, whereas cork appears to fail through core deformation and damage resistance rather than brittle fracture [N1-F1][N3-R3]. Damage progression is also an important difference: the review states that damage increases with repeated loading, while the cork study suggests improved damage resistance and damping, which may slow or reduce cumulative damage [N4-F3][N1-F1].

For low-velocity versus high-velocity suitability, the evidence is mixed but informative. The low-velocity impact review explicitly distinguishes low-velocity impact from high-velocity impact and notes that damage mechanisms and failure criteria differ across the two regimes [N2-F2]. It also states that high-performance sandwich structures commonly use carbon fiber face sheets with honeycomb or high-performance synthetic foam cores, while carbon fiber face sheets are used because of their outstanding specific strength [N2-F2]. The foam-core study notes that foam-core sandwich structures are preferred for bending, buckling, and energy absorption applications, including dynamic loading, high- and low-velocity impacts, blasts, crashes, etc. [N4-F3]. This suggests that foam cores are broadly useful for both low- and high-velocity impact, but that their performance depends on core density, face sheet thickness, and hybridization [N2-R3][N4-F3]. In contrast, the cork study says that cork agglomerates have beneficial energy absorption properties including noise mitigation, damping, and partial penetration low-velocity impact [N1-F1], implying that cork is more naturally suited to low-velocity impact scenarios where energy absorption and damping matter than to high-velocity regimes where brittle failure or penetration becomes dominant [N1-F1][N3-R3].

Overall, the evidence shows that foam cores can achieve relatively high peak loads and stiffness, but are vulnerable to brittle damage modes such as matrix cracking, foam cracking, and debonding [N4-F3][N3-R3]. Cork agglomerate sandwich composites appear to underperform in stiffness compared to synthetic foam cores, but excel in energy absorption, damping, and damage resistance [N1-F1][N1-R2]. Fiber-reinforced composites are important because they provide stiff face sheets, but their impact performance is still limited by poor impact resistance [N4-F3][N2-F2]. In short, for low-velocity impact, materials with higher energy absorption and damping are better; for high-velocity or penetration-dominated scenarios, materials with higher stiffness and damage tolerance may be preferred [N4-F3][N2-F2][N1-F1].

The evidence suggests that test conditions, specimen geometry, and measurement protocols strongly influence low-velocity impact results. The low-velocity impact review explicitly states that impact response is determined based on mass ratio, which is the ratio of impact mass to effective mass of the structural component, and that the response is subdivided into large, small, and medium mass impacts [N2-F2]. It also identifies impact duration as a key parameter for classifying low-velocity impact responses and exploring energy absorption characteristics [N2-F2]. This means that the same sandwich structure can produce different results depending on the drop mass, impact velocity, and energy level used. The review further notes that damage mechanisms and failure criteria differ, reinforcing that test conditions are central to interpreting results [N2-F2].

Specimen geometry also matters. The review states that sandwich structures are generally made of thin stiff face sheets separated by a lightweight, thick low-modulus core [N2-F2]. It also notes that the peak load and stiffness of the sandwich structure increase with relative density, panel thickness, and impact energy [N2-R3]. This implies that core thickness, face sheet thickness, and overall geometry can change how energy is absorbed, how stiff the structure behaves, and how much damage accumulates. The foam-core study similarly reports impact energy levels of 5 J, 10 J, 20 J, 30 J, and 40 J and uses different face sheet configurations to compare performance [N4-F3]. The evidence further notes that intra-ply and inter-ply hybrid face sheets can alter peak load and damage behavior [N4-F3], showing that geometry and hybridization are important variables.

Quasi-static versus dynamic testing is another key distinction. The low-velocity impact review explicitly contrasts low-velocity impact with high-velocity impact and emphasizes that dynamic response is central to the topic [N2-F2]. It also states that the first 150 years of impact study were devoted almost exclusively to empirical penetration studies, while later work moved toward semi-empirical and quasi-rational representations [N2-F2]. This indicates that quasi-static testing may not capture the true dynamic response of sandwich structures under impact. The review also states that the response of low-velocity impact is determined by mass ratio and that the response is subdivided into large, small, and medium mass impacts [N2-F2], which implies that dynamic loading conditions are more informative than static compression or bending tests for impact performance.

Limitations of extrapolating impact data to real-world use are clear in the evidence. The review notes that damage suffered internally during impact is very difficult to inspect [N2-F2]. It also says that impact failure is a common problem that affects strength and structural integrity, and that damage progressively increases with repeated loading [N4-F3]. The cork study further states that expanded cork showed improved impact damage resistance characteristics compared to synthetic foam, but also that its full potential in sandwich applications has not been thoroughly investigated [N1-F1]. Together, this suggests that laboratory impact data should be interpreted cautiously: real-world use may involve different impactors, velocities, energy levels, and environmental conditions that are not fully captured by controlled tests [N2-F2][N4-F3][N1-F1]. In addition, the evidence indicates that the same material can behave differently under different mass ratios and impact durations, so direct extrapolation from one test condition to another is unreliable [N2-F2][N2-R3].

In summary, the evidence shows that test conditions, geometry, and measurement protocol are major drivers of low-velocity impact results. Quasi-static results are not directly comparable to dynamic impact results, and real-world performance should not be assumed from laboratory data without accounting for mass ratio, impact duration, repeated loading, and internal damage visibility [N2-F2][N2-R3][N4-F3][N1-F1].

For honeycomb cores, the evidence is indirect rather than direct head-to-head. The review notes that high-performance sandwich structures commonly use carbon fiber face sheets with honeycomb cores made of Nomex, fiberglass reinforced thermoplastic, aluminium, and foam-type cores [N2-F2]. It also states that foam cores are used because of their high strength-to-weight ratio, good buckling resistance, and tailorable design, but that they are not ideal for energy absorption [N4-F3]. In comparison, the cork study emphasizes that cork agglomerates have beneficial energy absorption properties including noise mitigation, damping, and partial penetration low-velocity impact [N1-F1]. So while the evidence does not provide a direct honeycomb versus cork comparison, it does place honeycomb as a common high-performance core in aerospace applications, while cork is positioned as a more energy-absorptive, damping-enhancing alternative [N2-F2][N1-F1].

The evidence also includes foam-core benchmarking against hybrid face sheets. The foam-core study reports that the intra-ply hybrid foam core sandwich panel subjected to 40 J impact energy demonstrated a 13.17% higher maximum peak load compared to the carbon monolithic face sheet sandwich panel [N4-F3]. It also notes that the inter-ply hybrid foam core sandwich panel achieved a 31.57% higher maximum peak load than the carbon/kevlar-inverted face sheet configuration at 40 J [N4-F3]. This shows that hybridization and face sheet configuration can significantly affect peak load and damage behavior, but it does not directly compare cork to these hybrid systems. The study also says that sandwich structures suffer major damage from impact loads, and that damage progressively increases with repeated loading [N4-F3], which is an important limitation for direct comparison because real-world use often involves repeated impacts rather than single impacts.

Where cork excels relative to benchmark materials is in energy absorption, damping, and damage resistance, especially under low-velocity impact [N1-F1][N1-R2]. The evidence also suggests that cork can withstand higher impact forces than some thermoplastic foams [N6-R3]. Where cork underperforms is in stiffness: the cork study reports a decrease in bending stiffness compared to synthetic foam [N1-F1], and another source notes lower compressive stiffness compared to some synthetic cores [N6-R3]. The static flexural strength of synthetic foam composites was much higher than cork-core composites [N6-R4], which reinforces that cork is less stiff in static loading as well as in compressive stiffness.

Study limitations and why direct comparisons are ambiguous are several. First, the evidence spans different test conditions, specimen geometries, and face sheet configurations, so results are not fully comparable across studies [N2-F2][N4-F3]. Second, the cork study is explicit that expanded cork has not been properly studied in energy-absorption sandwich applications, and its full potential has not been thoroughly investigated [N1-F1]. Third, the foam-core evidence shows that peak load and damage behavior depend on face sheet hybridization, panel thickness, and impact energy [N4-F3][N2-R3]. Fourth, the review notes that internal damage is hard to inspect and that damage increases with repeated loading [N2-F2][N4-F3]. Finally, the evidence indicates that impact response is determined by mass ratio and impact duration, so the same material can behave differently under different dynamic conditions [N2-F2].

Overall, the direct comparative evidence suggests that cork agglomerate sandwich composites are a better fit for low-velocity impact scenarios where energy absorption and damping are important, while synthetic foams and honeycomb cores are often better at stiffness and peak load under controlled conditions [N1-F1][N4-F3][N2-F2]. However, direct head-to-head comparisons are limited by differences in test setup, face sheet design, and loading conditions, so the evidence should be interpreted cautiously [N2-F2][N4-F3][N1-F1].

## How cork agglomerate sandwich composites perform under low-velocity impact, compared to other materials

The evidence points to a clear but nuanced conclusion: **cork agglomerate sandwich composites perform well under low-velocity impact in terms of energy absorption and damping, but they generally underperform in stiffness compared to many synthetic foams and other high-performance cores** [N1-F1][N1-R2][N4-F3]. At the same time, other materials such as foam cores, honeycomb cores, and fiber-reinforced composites each have their own strengths and weaknesses, and direct comparisons are often ambiguous because of differences in test conditions, geometry, and loading protocols [N2-F2][N2-R3][N4-F3][N6-R2].

## 1) Performance of cork agglomerate sandwich composites under low-velocity impact

### Energy absorption capacity and force-displacement response
The direct evidence indicates that cork agglomerate sandwich composites are energy-absorptive. The study on expanded cork core-carbon fiber sandwiches reports that the sandwich plates absorb more energy because the cork core deforms, due to its low stiffness, and contributes to energy absorption [N1-R2]. The same source also emphasizes that cork is a 100% natural lightweight agglomerate material whose recovery properties are useful in energy absorption [N1-F1]. While the excerpt does not provide a full force-displacement curve, the implication is that cork’s low stiffness allows it to deform and absorb energy gradually during impact, which is consistent with a relatively soft or energy-absorptive force-displacement response [N1-R2].

### Stiffness and damping behavior
Stiffness and damping are directionally opposite for cork. The study reports that expanded cork showed a **decrease in bending stiffness** compared to synthetic foam, but a **large improvement in acoustic, damping, and impact damage resistance characteristics** [N1-F1]. That means cork is less stiff during impact, which can help spread the load over more core material, but it is better at dissipating vibrational energy and reducing residual vibrations [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that bending tests were used to examine stiffness and wavenumber and damping tests were used to characterize acoustic and vibrational damping [N1-F1]. So, in the context of low-velocity impact, cork’s performance is characterized by **lower stiffness but better damping** [N1-F1].

### Failure modes and relevance to performance
The failure behavior of cork agglomerate sandwich composites appears to be more progressive and damage-tolerant than brittle failure. The direct evidence states that cork agglomerates have beneficial energy absorption properties including noise mitigation, damping, and partial penetration low-velocity impact [N1-F1]. The evidence shows that benchmark materials vary widely in energy absorption and stiffness. This implies that stiffer cores can achieve higher stiffness, but energy absorption is not necessarily the same as stiffness. Failure behavior differs across materials. The foam-core study reports damage modes including **fiber breakage, matrix cracking, foam cracking, and debonding** [N4-F3]. The low-velocity impact review notes that common failure mechanisms include **matrix cracking, delaminations, foam crushing, or face–core debonding and perforation** [N3-R3]. These are consistent with brittle or progressive damage in foam and hybrid face sheet systems, whereas cork appears to fail through **core deformation and damage resistance** rather than brittle fracture [N1-F1][N3-R3]. Damage progression is also important: the review states that damage increases with repeated loading [N2-F2], while the cork study suggests improved damage resistance and damping [N1-F1]. This matters because many real-world applications involve repeated or cyclic loading rather than single impacts [N2-F2][N1-F1].

### Suitability for low-velocity vs high-velocity impact
The evidence is clear that materials are not universally best for one impact regime only. The low-velocity impact review explicitly distinguishes **low-velocity impact** from **high-velocity impact** and notes that damage mechanisms and failure criteria differ across the two regimes [N2-F2]. It also states that high-performance sandwich structures commonly use carbon fiber face sheets with honeycomb or high-performance synthetic foam cores [N2-F2]. The foam-core study notes that foam-core sandwich structures are preferred for bending, buckling, and energy absorption applications, including dynamic loading, high- and low-velocity impacts, blasts, crashes, etc. [N4-F3]. The most direct comparison in the evidence is between expanded cork and Rohacell® 110 IG synthetic foam. The study reports that expanded cork showed a **decrease in bending stiffness** compared to synthetic foam, but a **large improvement in acoustic, damping, and impact damage resistance characteristics** [N1-F1]. It also says that at this impact energy, the sandwich plates absorb more energy because the cork core deforms, due to its low stiffness, and contributes to energy absorption [N1-R2]. This head-to-head comparison suggests that cork is **less stiff than synthetic foam but better at energy absorption and damping** [N1-F1][N1-R2].

Another direct comparison is between agglomerated cork and PVC foam. It also states that foam cores are used because of their high strength-to-weight ratio, good buckling resistance, and tailorable design, but that they are not ideal for energy absorption [N4-F3]. In comparison, the cork study emphasizes that cork agglomerates have beneficial energy absorption properties including noise mitigation, damping, and partial penetration low-velocity impact [N1-F1]. So while the evidence does not provide a direct honeycomb versus cork comparison, it places honeycomb as a common high-performance core in aerospace applications, while cork is positioned as a more energy-absorptive, damping-enhancing alternative [N2-F2][N1-F1].

Where cork excels relative to benchmark materials is in **energy absorption, damping, and damage resistance**, especially under low-velocity impact [N1-F1][N1-R2]. Where cork underperforms is in **stiffness**: the cork study reports a decrease in bending stiffness compared to synthetic foam [N1-F1], and another source notes lower compressive stiffness compared to some synthetic cores [N6-R3]. Direct comparisons are limited by several factors. ## 4) Contextual factors that affect performance comparisons

### Test conditions and specimen geometry
The evidence shows that test conditions and specimen geometry strongly influence low-velocity impact results. The low-velocity impact review explicitly states that impact response is determined based on **mass ratio**, which is the ratio of impact mass to effective mass of the structural component, and that the response is subdivided into large, small, and medium mass impacts [N2-F2]. It also identifies **impact duration** as a key parameter for classifying low-velocity impact responses and exploring energy absorption characteristics [N2-F2]. This means that the same sandwich structure can produce different results depending on the drop mass, impact velocity, and energy level used. The review further notes that damage mechanisms and failure criteria differ, reinforcing that test conditions are central to interpreting results [N2-F2].

Specimen geometry also matters. The review states that sandwich structures are generally made of **thin stiff face sheets separated by a lightweight, thick low-modulus core** [N2-F2]. It also notes that the **peak load and stiffness** of the sandwich structure increase with **relative density, panel thickness, and impact energy** [N2-R3]. This implies that core thickness, face sheet thickness, and overall geometry can change how energy is absorbed, how stiff the structure behaves, and how much damage accumulates. Quasi-static versus dynamic testing is a major distinction. The low-velocity impact review explicitly contrasts low-velocity impact with high-velocity impact and emphasizes that dynamic response is central to the topic [N2-F2]. It also states that the first 150 years of impact study were devoted almost exclusively to empirical penetration studies, while later work moved toward semi-empirical and quasi-rational representations [N2-F2]. This indicates that quasi-static testing may not capture the true dynamic response of sandwich structures under impact. The review also states that the response of low-velocity impact is determined by mass ratio and that the response is subdivided into large, small, and medium mass impacts [N2-F2], which implies that dynamic loading conditions are more informative than static compression or bending tests for impact performance.

### Limitations of extrapolating impact data to real-world use
The evidence clearly warns against overgeneralizing from laboratory impact data to real-world use. The review notes that damage suffered internally during impact is very difficult to inspect [N2-F2]. It also says that impact failure is a common problem that affects strength and structural integrity, and that damage progressively increases with repeated loading [N4-F3]. The cork study further states that expanded cork showed improved impact damage resistance characteristics compared to synthetic foam, but also that its full potential in sandwich applications has not been thoroughly investigated [N1-F1]. Together, this suggests that laboratory impact data should be interpreted cautiously: real-world use may involve different impactors, velocities, energy levels, and environmental conditions that are not fully captured by controlled tests [N2-F2][N4-F3][N1-F1]. In addition, the evidence indicates that the same material can behave differently under different mass ratios and impact durations, so direct extrapolation from one test condition to another is unreliable [N2-F2][N2-R3].

---

## Final integrated conclusion

Overall, the evidence supports the following integrated conclusion: **cork agglomerate sandwich composites are a promising low-velocity impact material because they absorb energy well, exhibit good damping, and show damage resistance, but they generally sacrifice stiffness compared to many synthetic foams and hybrid cores** [N1-F1][N1-R2][N4-F3]. For **higher stiffness or peak-load scenarios**, synthetic foams and hybrid foam cores may be more suitable, but they can be less forgiving under repeated impact or brittle failure [N4-F3][N2-F2]. Damage progression is also important: the review states that damage increases with repeated loading [N2-F2], while the cork study suggests improved damage resistance and damping [N1-F1]. This matters because many real-world applications involve repeated or cyclic loading rather than single impacts [N2-F2][N1-F1].

### Suitability for low-velocity vs high-velocity impact
The evidence is clear that materials are not universally best for one impact regime only. The low-velocity impact review explicitly distinguishes **low-velocity impact** from **high-velocity impact** and notes that damage mechanisms and failure criteria differ across the two regimes [N2-F2]. It also states that high-performance sandwich structures commonly use carbon fiber face sheets with honeycomb or high-performance synthetic foam cores [N2-F2]. The foam-core study notes that foam-core sandwich structures are preferred for bending, buckling, and energy absorption applications, including dynamic loading, high- and low-velocity impacts, blasts, crashes, etc. [N4-F3]. This suggests that **foam cores are broadly useful for both low- and high-velocity impact**, but their performance depends on core density, face sheet thickness, and hybridization [N2-R3][N4-F3].

In contrast, the cork study emphasizes that cork agglomerates have beneficial energy absorption properties including **noise mitigation, damping, and partial penetration low-velocity impact** [N1-F1]. This implies that cork is more naturally suited to low-velocity impact scenarios where energy absorption and damping matter than to high-velocity regimes where brittle failure or penetration becomes dominant [N1-F1][N3-R3]. So, for low-velocity impact, materials with higher energy absorption and damping are better; for high-velocity or penetration-dominated scenarios, materials with higher stiffness and damage tolerance may be preferred [N4-F3][N2-F2][N1-F1].

## 3) Direct comparative evidence for cork vs foam/honeycomb and synthetic cores

### Head-to-head performance metrics
The most direct comparison in the evidence is between expanded cork and Rohacell® 110 IG synthetic foam. The study reports that expanded cork showed a **decrease in bending stiffness** compared to synthetic foam, but a **large improvement in acoustic, damping, and impact damage resistance characteristics** [N1-F1]. It also says that at this impact energy, the sandwich plates absorb more energy because the cork core deforms, due to its low stiffness, and contributes to energy absorption [N1-R2]. This head-to-head comparison suggests that cork is **less stiff than synthetic foam but better at energy absorption and damping** [N1-F1][N1-R2].

Another direct comparison is between agglomerated cork and PVC foam. A search result states that the main differences between agglomerated cork and PVC foam response arise when maximum force evolution is considered, and that agglomerated cork displays a different behavior [N6-R2]. It also notes that cork agglomerates are capable of withstanding higher impact forces than thermoplastic foams and have lower compressive stiffness compared to some other cores [N6-R3]. This implies that cork can be more impact-tolerant in some respects, but its lower compressive stiffness may be a drawback in other situations [N6-R3][N6-R2].

For honeycomb cores, the evidence is indirect rather than direct head-to-head. The review notes that high-performance sandwich structures commonly use carbon fiber face sheets with honeycomb cores made of Nomex, fiberglass reinforced thermoplastic, aluminium, and foam-type cores [N2-F2]. It also states that foam cores are used because of their high strength-to-weight ratio, good buckling resistance, and tailorable design, but that they are not ideal for energy absorption [N4-F3]. In comparison, the cork study emphasizes that cork agglomerates have beneficial energy absorption properties including noise mitigation, damping, and partial penetration low-velocity impact [N1-F1]. So while the evidence does not provide a direct honeycomb versus cork comparison, it places honeycomb as a common high-performance core in aerospace applications, while cork is positioned as a more energy-absorptive, damping-enhancing alternative [N2-F2][N1-F1].

### Where cork excels and underperforms
Where cork excels relative to benchmark materials is in **energy absorption, damping, and damage resistance**, especially under low-velocity impact [N1-F1][N1-R2]. The evidence also suggests that cork can withstand higher impact forces than some thermoplastic foams [N6-R3]. Where cork underperforms is in **stiffness**: the cork study reports a decrease in bending stiffness compared to synthetic foam [N1-F1], and another source notes lower compressive stiffness compared to some synthetic cores [N6-R3]. The static flexural strength of synthetic foam composites was much higher than cork-core composites [N6-R4], which reinforces that cork is less stiff in static loading as well as in compressive stiffness.

### Study limitations and why direct comparisons are ambiguous
Direct comparisons are limited by several factors. First, the evidence spans different test conditions, specimen geometries, and face sheet configurations, so results are not fully comparable across studies [N2-F2][N4-F3]. Second, the cork study is explicit that expanded cork has not been properly studied in energy-absorption sandwich applications, and its full potential has not been thoroughly investigated [N1-F1]. Third, the foam-core evidence shows that peak load and damage behavior depend on face sheet hybridization, panel thickness, and impact energy [N4-F3][N2-R3]. Fourth, the review notes that internal damage is hard to inspect and that damage increases with repeated loading [N2-F2][N4-F3]. Finally, the evidence indicates that impact response is determined by mass ratio and impact duration, so the same material can behave differently under different dynamic conditions [N2-F2].

## 4) Contextual factors that affect performance comparisons

### Test conditions and specimen geometry
The evidence shows that test conditions and specimen geometry strongly influence low-velocity impact results. The low-velocity impact review explicitly states that impact response is determined based on **mass ratio**, which is the ratio of impact mass to effective mass of the structural component, and that the response is subdivided into large, small, and medium mass impacts [N2-F2]. It also identifies **impact duration** as a key parameter for classifying low-velocity impact responses and exploring energy absorption characteristics [N2-F2]. This means that the same sandwich structure can produce different results depending on the drop mass, impact velocity, and energy level used. The review further notes that damage mechanisms and failure criteria differ, reinforcing that test conditions are central to interpreting results [N2-F2].

Specimen geometry also matters. The review states that sandwich structures are generally made of **thin stiff face sheets separated by a lightweight, thick low-modulus core** [N2-F2]. It also notes that the **peak load and stiffness** of the sandwich structure increase with **relative density, panel thickness, and impact energy** [N2-R3]. This implies that core thickness, face sheet thickness, and overall geometry can change how energy is absorbed, how stiff the structure behaves, and how much damage accumulates. The foam-core study similarly reports impact energy levels of 5 J, 10 J, 20 J, 30 J, and 40 J and uses different face sheet configurations to compare performance [N4-F3]. The evidence further notes that intra-ply and inter-ply hybrid face sheets can alter peak load and damage behavior [N4-F3], showing that geometry and hybridization are important variables.

### Quasi-static versus dynamic testing
Quasi-static versus dynamic testing is a major distinction. The low-velocity impact review explicitly contrasts low-velocity impact with high-velocity impact and emphasizes that dynamic response is central to the topic [N2-F2]. It also states that the first 150 years of impact study were devoted almost exclusively to empirical penetration studies, while later work moved toward semi-empirical and quasi-rational representations [N2-F2]. This indicates that quasi-static testing may not capture the true dynamic response of sandwich structures under impact. The review also states that the response of low-velocity impact is determined by mass ratio and that the response is subdivided into large, small, and medium mass impacts [N2-F2], which implies that dynamic loading conditions are more informative than static compression or bending tests for impact performance.

### Limitations of extrapolating impact data to real-world use
The evidence clearly warns against overgeneralizing from laboratory impact data to real-world use. The review notes that damage suffered internally during impact is very difficult to inspect [N2-F2]. It also says that impact failure is a common problem that affects strength and structural integrity, and that damage progressively increases with repeated loading [N4-F3]. The cork study further states that expanded cork showed improved impact damage resistance characteristics compared to synthetic foam, but also that its full potential in sandwich applications has not been thoroughly investigated [N1-F1]. Together, this suggests that laboratory impact data should be interpreted cautiously: real-world use may involve different impactors, velocities, energy levels, and environmental conditions that are not fully captured by controlled tests [N2-F2][N4-F3][N1-F1]. In addition, the evidence indicates that the same material can behave differently under different mass ratios and impact durations, so direct extrapolation from one test condition to another is unreliable [N2-F2][N2-R3].

## Final integrated conclusion

Overall, the evidence supports the following integrated conclusion: **cork agglomerate sandwich composites are a promising low-velocity impact material because they absorb energy well, exhibit good damping, and show damage resistance, but they generally sacrifice stiffness compared to many synthetic foams and hybrid cores** [N1-F1][N1-R2][N4-F3]. Other benchmark materials such as foam cores and hybrid face sheet configurations can achieve higher peak loads and stiffness, but they are also more prone to brittle failure modes such as matrix cracking, foam crushing, and debonding [N4-F3][N3-R3]. Honeycomb cores are used in high-performance aerospace applications but are not explicitly shown here as a direct cork competitor, while the evidence suggests they are still part of the broader family of high-performance cores [N2-F2]. 

In practice, the best choice depends on the application. For **low-velocity impact scenarios**, cork agglomerate is attractive because it is energy-absorptive, damping-enhancing, and damage-tolerant [N1-F1][N1-R2]. For **higher stiffness or peak-load scenarios**, synthetic foams and hybrid foam cores may be more suitable, but they can be less forgiving under repeated impact or brittle failure [N4-F3][N2-F2]. The evidence also shows that **direct comparisons are ambiguous** because test conditions, geometry, and loading protocols vary widely across studies [N2-F2][N4-F3][N6-R2].
